passage:
At a pavement café in Barcelona, Xin started rubbing her eyes with both fists and pushing her face into Lucia's chest.
"Sleepy already?" Lucia checked the time. Xin had napped well that morning. The street was quiet. But lunch had been small and early.
Lucia took a rice cake from her bag. Xin grabbed it, ate it in four bites, and sat up straight, bright-eyed, pointing at the pigeons.

qa.q: What did Lucia take from her bag?
qa.a: A rice cake.

qa.q: What was Xin most likely feeling when she rubbed her eyes, and what else might it have been?
qa.a: She was most likely hungry, since she perked up after eating; it could also have been tiredness, but Xin had napped well that morning, so Lucia ruled that out.

qa.q: Which choice of Lucia's worked, and why?
qa.a: Checking the nap, the noise and the lunch before deciding worked, because it led her to the real need, hunger.

qa.q: What would change if Lucia had assumed Xin was sleepy?
qa.a: She might have tried to put her down for a rest, and Xin would have stayed hungry and fussy.

grounding: A mother reads her toddler's eye-rubbing by checking nap, noise and food, and finds hunger rather than sleep.

passage: I'm Tarun, and I thought my little brother Mohit was just sleepy that evening. He kept tugging his right ear and rubbing his eyes, and he pushed his face into Mummy's neck. But it was only six o'clock. Mummy felt his forehead and cheeks and said he was warm. She didn't wait to see. She rang the doctor that evening and took him in. I was wrong about the sleepy part. You can't tell from one sign.

qa.q: Which ear did Mohit keep tugging?
qa.a: His right ear.

qa.q: What was Mohit likely feeling as he tugged his ear and pushed his face into Mummy's neck?
qa.a: He was likely unwell and uncomfortable, perhaps in pain, and wanted comfort; tiredness was possible, but it was early and he felt warm.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that was wise?
qa.a: She checked the whole picture, the time and his warm forehead, and rang the doctor that same evening instead of waiting.

qa.q: How does Tarun see the evening afterwards?
qa.a: Tarun realises the first guess was wrong and learns that one sign isn't enough to know what's going on.

grounding: A brother learns that his toddler brother's ear-tugging and eye-rubbing meant feeling unwell, as their mother checked the whole picture.

passage:
Monday, one o'clock: Kalyani rubbed her eyes and leaned on Vikas's leg. It was nap time. He took her to bed and she slept at once.
Thursday, at a loud birthday party: she rubbed her eyes again and hid her face. It wasn't nap time. Vikas carried her out to the quiet hallway, and she brightened.
Saturday evening, dinner was late: eye-rubbing, whining. Vikas gave her a banana, and she stopped.

qa.q: What did Vikas give Kalyani on Saturday evening?
qa.a: A banana.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling each time she rubbed her eyes?
qa.a: On Monday she was tired, on Thursday overwhelmed by the loud party, and on Saturday hungry; the same cue carried different feelings.

qa.q: What habit helped Vikas respond well?
qa.a: He looked at the time, the place and what she had eaten each time, rather than assuming one meaning.

qa.q: What would change if Vikas had always put Kalyani to bed when she rubbed her eyes?
qa.a: He would have missed that she was overwhelmed or hungry on other days, and she would have stayed upset.

grounding: Over a week a father learns that his toddler's eye-rubbing can mean tired, overwhelmed or hungry, and checks the whole picture.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. At story time Amandeep sat with his thumb in his mouth and twirled a lock of hair over his ear. When a younger child started crying, the twirling got faster. A visiting parent asked if I should stop him. I didn't. It seems to help him settle when he is tired or worried. I put his soft blanket beside him, and after the story he took the thumb out by himself to point at the pictures. Eshaan, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Eshaan put beside Amandeep?
qa.a: His soft blanket.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have been feeling when the twirling got faster?
qa.a: He was probably worried or unsettled by the younger child crying, and the thumb and hair-twirling were helping him calm down.

qa.q: How could Eshaan answer the visiting parent's question?
qa.a: By explaining that thumb-sucking and hair-twirling are ordinary comforts at this age and that shaming or stopping them doesn't help.

qa.q: How might the visiting parent see the thumb-sucking?
qa.a: The parent may think it is a habit to be stopped, rather than a way Amandeep settles himself.

grounding: A teacher sees a toddler suck his thumb and twirl his hair when worried or tired, and lets the comfort be without shaming.

passage:
The bus to the district town was late, and the stand was hot and crowded. Binita sat on her Dadi's lap, thumb in her mouth, winding a curl of her hair round and round one finger.
"Chhi, dirty habit," an aunty on the bench said. "Take it out, girl."
Urmila, her Dadi, just shifted Binita closer. "She's tired. It calms her. She'll grow out of it." Binita's eyelids drooped, the finger still turning slowly.

qa.q: What was Binita winding round her finger?
qa.a: A curl of her hair.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling as she sucked her thumb and wound her hair?
qa.a: She was tired and probably uncomfortable in the hot, crowded bus stand, and was soothing herself; her drooping eyelids show she was settling.

qa.q: Which reaction helped Binita more, and why?
qa.a: Urmila's calm acceptance helped, because it let Binita keep her comfort without being shamed.

qa.q: How does the aunty see the thumb-sucking?
qa.a: The aunty sees it as dirty and wants it stopped, not as a tired child's way of calming down.

grounding: A grandmother lets her toddler granddaughter suck her thumb and twirl her hair for comfort, refusing to shame her.

passage:
It was their first night in the new house in Lima. Rosa lay in her cot, wide awake, stroking the satin edge of her old blanket between finger and thumb, over and over.
Daniel sat by the cot. He didn't take the blanket or tell her to sleep. He just sat.
The stroking went on for a long time. Then it slowed. Rosa's thumb found her mouth, her eyes closed, and the blanket stayed bunched under her chin.

qa.q: What did Rosa stroke between finger and thumb?
qa.a: The satin edge of her old blanket.

qa.q: What was Rosa likely feeling on the first night in the new house?
qa.a: She was likely unsettled and a little worried in a strange room, and stroking the familiar blanket helped her feel safe enough to sleep.

qa.q: What did Daniel do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed nearby and left the blanket with her, letting her use her own comfort without rushing her.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel as Rosa finally falls asleep?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and tender, knowing the move was hard for her too. 🤍

grounding: A toddler strokes her blanket and sucks her thumb to settle on a worrying first night, and her father lets the comfort be.

passage:
Thunder cracked over the Oslo rooftops. Lars dropped his train and climbed straight into Oskar's lap, pushing his face into his grandfather's jumper.
Oskar wrapped both arms round him and hummed. Lars stayed curled up, holding a fold of wool in his fist.
When the rain softened, Lars wriggled and pushed at Oskar's arm. Oskar opened his arms at once, and Lars slid down to find his train.

qa.q: What did Lars drop when the thunder cracked?
qa.a: His train.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when he climbed into Oskar's lap?
qa.a: He was frightened by the thunder and wanted closeness and safety; wriggling down later shows he felt calm again.

qa.q: Which of Oskar's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Holding him warmly during the thunder and opening his arms at once when Lars pushed away worked, because both the need for comfort and the wish to go were respected.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel when Lars slides off his lap?
qa.a: He probably feels content, glad he could be a safe place and that Lars felt ready to play again.

grounding: A toddler climbs into his grandfather's lap for comfort in a storm, and is let go when he pulls away.

passage: I'm Hrithik, Chandrika's big brother. At the crowded Sunday market, she grabbed my hand and wouldn't let go, even to point at the balloons. At home, she climbed into Papa's lap and curled up like a cat. But when our uncle came and tried to hug her, she pushed his chest and turned away. Mummy said, "Let her be, she'll come when she wants." Uncle laughed and let go. I don't know why she didn't want him. Maybe she was just full up on hugs.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do when their uncle tried to hug her?
qa.a: She pushed his chest and turned away.

qa.q: What might Chandrika have been feeling at the market and in Papa's lap?
qa.a: She was likely a bit anxious in the crowd and sought safety by holding Hrithik's hand, and she felt comfortable and secure curled up in Papa's lap.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that respected Chandrika?
qa.a: She let Chandrika refuse the hug and said she would come when she wanted, instead of making her hug.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Chandrika pushes him away?
qa.a: He might feel a little hurt, but he laughed and let go, respecting her choice.

grounding: A brother sees his toddler sister seek touch from family for comfort and pull away from a hug, and their mother respects it.

passage:
The day Mumma came home from hospital with the new baby, Ritu climbed into Hrithik's lap and would not leave it, even to eat.
Four days later, she sat beside him, holding his hand tight, watching Mumma feed the baby.
By the second week, Ritu leaned against him for a quick cuddle, then wriggled off his lap to go and bang her drum. Hrithik let her go, smiling.

qa.q: What did Ritu go to do in the second week?
qa.a: She wriggled off Hrithik's lap to go and bang her drum.

qa.q: What was Ritu likely feeling on the day the new baby came home?
qa.a: She was likely unsettled and a bit worried about the change, and staying in Hrithik's lap made her feel safe.

qa.q: What helped Ritu feel secure again?
qa.a: Hrithik's steady, warm closeness whenever she sought it, and letting her go when she was ready.

qa.q: How might Mumma see Ritu clinging to Hrithik?
qa.a: She may feel grateful that Ritu has a safe lap while she is busy with the baby, and perhaps a pang that she can't hold Ritu as much. 🤍

grounding: Over two weeks a toddler seeks her father's lap and hand for comfort after a new baby arrives, and he lets her go when she is ready.

passage:
In the courtyard of their village house, Devika's cousin grabbed her little cloth ball. Devika screamed, shoved him, and then hit his arm.
Manjula, her mother, came over quickly and calmly, holding Devika's hand. "You're angry. He took your ball. I won't let you hit." She stroked the cousin's arm softly with Devika's hand. "Gentle hands. Say, 'Mine.'"
Devika glared, then said, "Mine!" The cousin handed the ball back.

qa.q: What did Devika's cousin grab?
qa.a: Her little cloth ball.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she shoved and hit her cousin?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated that her ball was taken, and she didn't yet have the words to say so.

qa.q: What made Manjula's response wise?
qa.a: She stayed calm, stopped the hitting, named the anger, showed gentle hands and gave Devika a word to use.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Devika says "Mine!"?
qa.a: The cousin may feel a bit surprised, but hearing the word makes it clearer and easier to give the ball back.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's hitting with calm limits, a named feeling, gentle hands and a word to use.

passage:
In the sandpit at a Dublin park, a boy took Liam's red spade. Liam pushed him hard, and the boy sat down in the sand.
Freya, Liam's mother, knelt between them. She held Liam's hands firmly, not roughly. "You're cross. You wanted your spade. I won't let you push." She turned to the boy. "Are you okay?"
Then to Liam: "Say, 'My turn.'"
"My tun!" Liam shouted. The boy held out the spade.

qa.q: What colour was Liam's spade?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he pushed the boy?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated that his spade was taken, and he had no words ready to say so.

qa.q: What did Freya do well?
qa.a: She held his hands firmly but calmly, named his feeling, checked on the other boy and gave Liam words to use instead of pushing.

qa.q: How might the boy experience being pushed?
qa.a: He was likely shocked and hurt, and Freya's check helped him feel noticed.

grounding: A toddler pushes when his toy is taken, and his mother sets a calm limit, names the feeling and teaches words.

passage: I'm Rafiq, from the flat opposite, and I was at their door on Friday when it happened. Asif's mother took a pair of scissors away from him, and he hit her arm, hard, screaming. I expected her to shout. She didn't. She caught his hand and held it. "You're angry. You wanted those. I won't let you hit." He kicked and cried. She waited, holding on. After a bit, he slumped against her.

qa.q: What did Asif's mother take away from him?
qa.a: A pair of scissors.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he hit his mother's arm?
qa.a: He was probably angry and frustrated at losing the scissors, not trying to be cruel; slumping against her later suggests he was worn out and needed comfort.

qa.q: Which of the mother's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm, holding his hand and naming the feeling worked, because it set a limit without adding more anger.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see the mother's reaction?
qa.a: Rafiq is surprised, having expected shouting, and seems impressed by her calm.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler hit in frustration and his mother answer with a calm limit and named feeling.

subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
passage: At the Lodhi Garden lawn in Delhi, Dolma toddled off toward the flowerbed. Halfway there, she stopped and looked back at Devika, her nanny, on the bench. Devika waved. Dolma ran back, patted Devika's knee once, then set off again, farther this time, to the fountain. She looked back again. Another wave. This time she didn't come back, just smiled and kept watching the water.

qa.q: Where did Dolma go the second time?
qa.a: To the fountain.

qa.q: Why did Dolma keep looking back at Devika?
qa.a: She wanted to check Devika was still there, which made her feel safe enough to explore farther; she seemed confident and happy.

qa.q: What could Devika keep doing to support Dolma's exploring?
qa.a: Stay in sight, wave back each time Dolma checks, and keep watch as Dolma goes farther.

qa.q: How might Devika feel as Dolma explores farther?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased at Dolma's growing confidence, while keeping a close eye on her near the water.

grounding: A toddler explores away from her nanny and checks back for reassurance, showing trust and safe-base seeking.

subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
passage:
"Santosh, where's Kunal?"
"There, by the bangle stall. He keeps coming back to touch my leg, then off again."
"Good. He's checking on us."
"Now he's going round the corner."
"Did he look back?"
"No. Not once."
"Go. Now."
Santosh walked quickly after him and scooped Kunal up by the balloon cart. "You went too far, little one. Stay where you can see Papa."
Kunal laughed and pointed at the balloons.

qa.q: Where did Santosh scoop Kunal up?
qa.a: By the balloon cart.

qa.q: What might Kunal have been feeling when he went round the corner without looking back?
qa.a: He was probably excited and curious about the stalls and not worried at all, which is why he stopped checking back.

qa.q: Why did Santosh go after him quickly?
qa.a: Because Kunal had stopped looking back, which meant he needed close supervision in the crowd.

qa.q: How might Kunal's mother have felt when he went round the corner?
qa.a: She was likely worried and alarmed, which is why she told Santosh to go at once.

grounding: Parents notice their toddler's checking back and act quickly when he wanders off without it, since he needs supervision.

subtype: Approaching and staying near a caregiver [Expressing]
passage: Childminder's note, Wednesday. At the park Sunaina did her usual loop: out to the sandpit, back to touch my knee, out to the swings, back again. Around mid-morning she walked toward the gate and did not look back once. I followed her straight away and brought her back to the sandpit. She was happy, not upset. I will stay closer when she is near the gate, as she doesn't seem to check when she gets excited. Bhavna, childminder

qa.q: What did Sunaina do each time she came back?
qa.a: She came back to touch the childminder's knee.

qa.q: What was Sunaina likely feeling when she walked toward the gate?
qa.a: She was probably curious and excited, and in that mood she forgot to check back, rather than trying to run off.

qa.q: What did Bhavna plan to do differently?
qa.a: To stay closer when Sunaina is near the gate, since she doesn't check back when excited.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel reassured that Bhavna noticed quickly and has a plan to keep her safe.

grounding: A childminder notes a toddler's pattern of returning for reassurance and supervises closely when she wanders off without checking.

passage: Creche note, first week. When I came to say hello, Ayesha turned her face into her father's chest and would not look at me. I did not reach for her. I sat on the rug a little way off and put together a wooden fish puzzle, talking to her father. After a while she turned her head to watch. Later she crawled over and handed me the last piece. Joseph, creche teacher

qa.q: What puzzle did Joseph put together?
qa.a: A wooden fish puzzle.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she turned her face into her father's chest?
qa.a: She felt wary of a new person, not rude; watching and later bringing the piece shows she felt safer as trust grew.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting a little way off and not reaching for her worked, because it let Ayesha come closer on her own terms.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's father see her turning away?
qa.a: He probably understands she is wary with new people and may feel reassured that Joseph was patient with her.

grounding: A teacher waits and keeps a gentle distance when a toddler turns away from him, letting her approach in her own time.

passage:
The anganwadi worker, Yamini, came to the village house with her register. Avni took one look and turned her face into her Dadi's sari, gripping a fistful of it.
"Come, beta, say namaste," Dadi coaxed.
Yamini sat down on the far end of the cot. "No need. I'll just talk to Dadi." She filled her register and chatted. Soon Avni's face slid out from the sari, and she stared at Yamini's pen.

qa.q: What did Yamini bring to the house?
qa.a: Her register.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she turned into her Dadi's sari?
qa.a: She was wary and a little afraid of a new person, and turned to her Dadi for safety.

qa.a: Dadi seems to want Avni to be polite and say namaste, rather than seeing a child's normal wariness.

passage:
Abebe, the new neighbour in the Addis Ababa building, bent down and held out his hand. "Hello, little one!" Jin turned sharply away and pressed his face into his mother's legs.
Abebe straightened up and stepped back. He crouched by the stairs, a few steps off, and waved his fingers. "Okay. Another day."
Jin peeked out at the waving fingers, then hid again. Then peeked.

qa.q: Where did Abebe crouch after stepping back?
qa.a: By the stairs, a few steps off.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when he turned away and pressed his face into his mother's legs?
qa.a: He was wary of a stranger coming so close, and hid for safety; his peeking shows curiosity starting to grow.

qa.q: What did Abebe do that helps trust grow?
qa.a: He stepped back, kept a gentle distance and gave Jin time, saying "Another day."

qa.q: How might Jin's mother feel about Abebe's response?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that he didn't push or take offence.

passage:
Monday: Nirmala pulled a silly face at breakfast. Yogesh gave a small, surprised giggle.
Wednesday: she pulled the face again, and when he giggled, she giggled too. He laughed harder, and they both ended up breathless.
Friday: she tickled him, and kept going. His giggle turned high and shrill, his eyes went wide, and he pushed her hand away. Nirmala stopped at once and held him. "Too much? Okay."

qa.q: What made Yogesh giggle on Monday?
qa.a: Nirmala pulled a silly face at breakfast.

qa.q: What tells you Yogesh felt uneasy during the tickling on Friday?
qa.a: His giggle turned high and shrill, his eyes went wide and he pushed her hand away, signs that the laughter had become nervous or overwhelmed rather than delighted.

qa.a: Stopping at once and holding him worked, because she read his cues and made him feel safe again.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel after Friday's tickling?
qa.a: She might feel a little sorry for going too far, and glad she noticed his cues quickly.

grounding: Over a week a mother sees shared giggles grow and learns to spot when a toddler's laugh turns nervous.

passage:
On the stairs of their Kolkata building, Rafiq from the second floor hid behind the pillar and peeped out. "Boo!" Bidisha giggled. Again. Bigger giggle.
The third time, Rafiq jumped out fast and loud. Bidisha laughed, but it came out short and sharp, and she grabbed her Ma's dupatta.
Rafiq softened at once. He peeped out slowly, quietly. "boo." Bidisha's easy giggle came back.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq hide?
qa.a: Behind the pillar on the stairs.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when her laugh came out short and she grabbed Ma's dupatta?
qa.a: She was startled and a little nervous at the loud jump, even though she laughed; grabbing Ma showed she needed safety.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that kept the game happy?
qa.a: He noticed the change and made his peekaboo slow and quiet again, so her relaxed giggle returned.

qa.q: How might Ma see the moment?
qa.a: She would likely feel Bidisha grab her dupatta and be glad that Rafiq noticed and softened.

grounding: A toddler giggles at peekaboo, and a neighbour notices when a loud version turns her laugh nervous.

passage:
"Again!" Binita shrieked, and Rekha Masi tickled her tummy.
Binita giggled so hard she hiccupped.
"Is she laughing or does she want me to stop?" Rekha asked Binita's mother.
"Watch her hands."
Binita grabbed Rekha's fingers and pulled them back to her tummy. "Again!"

"No shame, laughing when she falls!" said her aunt.
Mohit stayed calm, crouched, and checked her hands and back. "Bump! Up you get." Anjali held out her arms, still giggling.

subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]

Sofia smiled calmly. "Big crash! Are you okay?" Marek's laugh softened into a real grin. He started building again.

subtype: Laughing at a fall or a shock [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Neelam, from next door. On Saturday little Jaya missed the last step of her porch and bumped down onto the path. She looked straight at her father, then started to laugh. Her father gasped loudly and rushed at her, "Oh no, oh no!" Jaya's laugh stopped. Her face crumpled and she wailed. I wonder if she'd have kept laughing if he'd stayed calm. She wasn't bleeding, just shocked.

qa.a: Onto the path, after missing the last step of her porch.

qa.q: What might Jaya's laugh before she cried have meant?

qa.a: Stay calm, check her quietly for injury and then comfort her, so she can read the moment as safe.

qa.q: How might Jaya's father have felt when she fell?

qa.a: A banana and a water cup.

qa.q: What was Daniel feeling when he bawled at the gate?
qa.a: He was very hungry and probably tired and upset from the delay, and his loud crying was his strongest signal that he needed help.

qa.q: Which choice of Elif's worked, and why?
qa.a: Responding quickly with food and a close hold worked, because it met the real need and calmed him.

qa.q: How might the other passengers see the bawling?
qa.a: Some may feel annoyed by the noise, while others might sympathise with a hungry child on a long delay.

subtype: Bawling from distress or unmet need [Expressing]
passage: I'm Chetan, and our flat shares a wall with Mehak's family. Late on Tuesday night, during the thunder, I heard her bawling, a big, wild cry. I couldn't tell if she was hurt or scared. Within a minute, I heard her father's footsteps, a light click on, and his voice low and slow. The bawling turned into sobs, then quiet hiccups. By the next thunderclap, the flat was silent.

qa.q: What was happening outside on Tuesday night?
qa.a: There was thunder.

Wednesday: a sudden sharp scream. Tanuja had caught her finger in the drawer. Seema ran to her and held the finger under cool water.
Saturday evening: a low, grizzling cry, eyes rubbed. Seema took her to bed.

qa.q: What did Seema give Tanuja on Monday?

qa.a: The rising whine on Monday meant hunger, the sharp scream on Wednesday meant pain, and the low grizzle on Saturday meant she was tired.

qa.q: What habit helped Seema respond well?
qa.a: Listening to the sound of each cry and looking at the situation, then responding promptly to the need.

qa.q: What would change if Seema treated all crying as "attention-seeking"?
qa.a: She would miss the real needs, and Tanuja would learn that crying doesn't bring help.

grounding: Over a week a mother learns that her toddler's different cries signal hunger, pain and tiredness, and responds promptly.

In their Kochi flat, Ira started crying from the living room, a cross, frustrated cry.
"Don't run every time, Jomon," said his uncle. "She's playing you."
Jomon went anyway. Ira was on her tummy, arm stretched under the sofa, her ball just out of reach. He fished it out. She took it, cried two more sobs, and stopped, rolling it back to him.

qa.q: Where was Ira's ball?
qa.a: Under the sofa, just out of reach.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she cried?
qa.a: She was frustrated that she couldn't reach her ball, and her cry was a way to ask for help.

qa.q: What would you advise Jomon's uncle?
qa.a: That a toddler's cry usually signals a real need, and checking quickly, as Jomon did, builds trust.

qa.q: How does the uncle see Ira's crying?
qa.a: He sees it as a trick to get attention, not a call for help.

grounding: A father answers his toddler's frustrated cry and finds a real need, not manipulation.

subtype: Crying as a signal of need [Expressing]
passage:
"Let him cry, Ankita. He'll learn."
"Learn what, Mummy? Something's wrong. Listen, that's his scared cry."
Ankita went to the window. A dog was barking loudly in the lane below, and Sahil was pressed against the wall, crying.
"Come here." She lifted him and turned away from the window. "Loud dog. You're safe."
Sahil hid his face in her neck and the crying faded.
"Hm," said his grandmother. "Scared cry. I didn't hear it."

qa.q: What was barking in the lane below?
qa.a: A dog.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling as he pressed against the wall?
qa.a: He was scared of the loud dog barking, and his crying was a signal that he needed help.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Going to him promptly and moving him away from the window worked, because it met his real need for safety.

qa.q: How does Sahil's grandmother see things by the end?
qa.a: She seems to accept that the crying had a real reason, noticing she hadn't heard it as a scared cry.

grounding: A mother recognises her toddler's scared cry as a signal of need and responds warmly rather than letting him cry.
